title: Applications of Statics, Including Problem-Solving Strategies
lead: Statics is Newton’s laws applied to a system that does not accelerate, and this section turns the two conditions for equilibrium into a method you can follow. It sets out four steps, among them the choice of a pivot point that makes the torque of an unknown force zero, and then works them through for a pole vaulter holding a pole three ways: with the center of gravity halfway between his hands, nearer one hand, and beyond both hands, where one hand has to push down instead of up.
objectives: Discuss the applications of Statics in real life.
State and discuss various problem-solving strategies in Statics.
summary_html: • Statics can be applied to a variety of situations, ranging from raising a drawbridge to bad posture and back strain. We have discussed the problem-solving strategies specifically useful for statics. Statics is a special case of Newton’s laws, both the general problem-solving strategies and the special strategies for Newton’s laws, discussed in Problem-Solving Strategies, still apply.

exercises.prompt: When visiting some countries, you may see a person balancing a load on the head. Explain why the center of mass of the load needs to be directly above the person’s neck vertebrae.

answer.solution: Treat the load as the system and take the pivot at the neck vertebrae, where the force that supports the load acts. That force is applied at the pivot, so its lever arm is zero and it exerts no torque about it. The only other force on the load is its weight, which acts at the load’s center of mass. If the center of mass sits directly above the vertebrae, the line along which the weight acts passes through the pivot, the perpendicular lever arm is zero as well, and the net torque on the load is zero without anything else having to act. Move the center of mass to one side and the weight gains a lever arm, so it produces a torque that turns the load off the head, and the muscles of the neck have to supply an equal and opposite torque to keep it there. Those muscles are attached very close to the joint, so their lever arms are short and the forces they must exert are large. Carrying the load with its center of mass over the vertebrae is therefore the one position in which the second condition for equilibrium is satisfied by itself.

exercises.prompt:
A 10 N board of uniform density is 5 meters long. It is supported on the left by a string bearing a 3 N upward force. In order to prevent the string from breaking, a person must place an upward force of 7 N at a position along the bottom surface of the board. At what distance from its left edge would they need to place this force in order for the board to be in static equilibrium?
  1. $\frac{3}{7}$ m
  2. $\frac{5}{2}$ m
  3. $\frac{25}{7}$ m
  4. $\frac{30}{7}$ m
  5. 5 m

answer.solution: Draw a free body diagram of the board and label the three forces with the places they are applied: the string pulls up with 3 N at the left edge, the board’s weight of 10 N acts down at its center of gravity, and the person pushes up with 7 N at the distance the question asks for. The board is of uniform density, so its center of gravity is at its middle, 2.5 m from the left edge. Now choose the pivot to simplify the solution. Putting it at the left edge makes the string’s lever arm zero, so the string’s torque drops out and only two torques are left: the weight turns the board one way about that point and the person’s force turns it the other. Setting them equal gives $(7\ \text{N})d = (10\ \text{N})(2.5\ \text{m})$, and solving for $d$ gives the distance from the left edge. Check the first condition as well: the two upward forces already add to the 10 N weight whatever $d$ is, so it is the second condition alone that decides where the hand goes, and the answer must be a distance that lies on the board.

exercises.prompt:
A bridge is supported by two piers located 20 meters apart. Both the left and right piers provide an upward force on the bridge, labeled $\kFL$ and $\kFR$ respectively.
  1. If a 1000 kg car comes to rest at a point 5 meters from the left pier, how much force will the bridge provide to the left and right piers?
  2. How will $\kFL$ and $\kFR$ change as the car drives to the right side of the bridge?

parts.hint: Take the pivot at the right pier, so that the right pier’s force has no lever arm and drops out. The car’s weight is $mg$ and it acts 15 m from that pivot.
The first condition for equilibrium gives the second force once the first is known: the two pier forces add to the weight of the car.

answer.solution: $\kFL = 7350\ \text{N}$ and $\kFR = 2450\ \text{N}$. As the car moves to the right side of the bridge, $\kFL$ will decrease and $\kFR$ will increase. At exactly halfway across the bridge, $\kFL$ and $\kFR$ will both be 4900 N.

exercises.prompt: An object of unknown mass is provided to a student. Without using a scale, design an experimental procedure detailing how the magnitude of this mass could be experimentally found. Your explanation must include the concept of torque and all steps should be provided in an orderly sequence. You may include a labeled diagram of your setup to help in your description. Include enough detail so that another student could carry out your procedure.

answer.solution: Make a balance out of a uniform rod and a knife edge, and use a known mass as the standard. First rest the rod on the knife edge with nothing hanging from it and slide it until it balances. The rod is then supported at its own center of gravity, so the rod’s weight is applied at the pivot, its lever arm is zero, and it exerts no torque in anything that follows. Hang the unknown mass from one side of the rod at a distance $r_1$ from the knife edge and the known mass from the other side at a distance $r_2$, and slide the known mass along the rod until the rod balances again. The rod is now in static equilibrium: its acceleration is zero and it is not rotating, so the net torque about the knife edge is zero and the two torques are equal and opposite, $m_1 g r_1 = m_2 g r_2$. The acceleration due to gravity is the same on both sides and cancels, so the unknown mass is $m_1 = m_2 r_2 / r_1$. Measure both distances from the knife edge to the point at which each mass hangs, repeat the balancing two or three times and average the readings, and check that the answer is reasonable: the heavier of the two masses must sit closer to the knife edge, and the mass you find should have the units of a mass and a size a hand can judge.
